corpus_definition: a good feeling you get when something meets your needs or wishes

forms.definition: the pleasant feeling you get when you have what you wanted
forms.example: She felt great satisfaction when her students passed the exam.

syn.note: Pleasure is any happy feeling; satisfaction comes when a wish or need is met.
A calm, happy feeling that lasts; a little more formal.
A deep feeling of happiness from doing something important. American spelling: fulfillment.
Easy, general word for feeling good.

ant.note: The feeling of not being pleased because something is not as good as you wanted.
The sad feeling when something is worse than you hoped.

forms.definition: to give someone what they want or need so they feel pleased
forms.example: Nothing satisfies my grandmother more than a full table of guests.

syn.note: Easy word: to make someone happy.
Formal: 'content yourself with' means accept something smaller.
Formal: to give someone pleasure.

ant.note: To make someone sad because something is not as good as they hoped.
Rare, formal: to fail to give someone what they want.

forms.definition: pleased because you have got what you wanted
forms.example: Are you satisfied with your new flat in Tashkent?
forms.note: satisfied with + noun: satisfied with the result.

syn.note: Easy and very close: 'pleased with'.
Everyday word: 'I'm happy with the result.'
Calm and happy with what you have.

ant.note: Not pleased because something is not good enough.
Easy word: not pleased.

forms.definition: giving you a pleasant feeling because it meets your needs
forms.example: It was a satisfying meal after a long day at work.

syn.note: Used for work or activities that make you feel good.
Giving pleasure; a little formal.
Easy word: nice to do.

ant.note: Not giving you a pleasant feeling; leaving you wanting more.
Not as good as you hoped.

forms.definition: good enough, but not excellent
forms.example: Your work this term is satisfactory.
forms.note: Belongs to satisfy = meet a standard or need, not the good feeling.

forms.definition: in a way that gives you a pleasant feeling
forms.example: The cake was satisfyingly sweet.
forms.note: Less common than the adjectives.

syn.note: In a way that gives pleasure; a little formal.
Easy word: in a good or pleasant way.

forms.definition: in a way that is good enough
forms.example: The problem was solved satisfactorily.
forms.note: Belongs to satisfy = meet a standard or need, not the good feeling.

context.text: Dilnoza felt real satisfaction when her first cake came out perfect. Her family was satisfied, and the smell alone was satisfying.

reviewer_note: Satisfactory/satisfactorily belong to the 'good enough' meaning (separate map), shown here as other_meaning. Opposites with dis-/un- are in ant lists.

corpus_definition: good enough but not excellent; meeting the basic required standard

forms.definition: the act of meeting a need, rule or standard
forms.example: The repairs were finished to the satisfaction of the building inspector.
forms.note: This use is formal: 'to someone's satisfaction'. The everyday meaning is the good feeling.

syn.note: Formal: meeting a need or doing what was promised. American spelling: fulfillment.

forms.definition: to be good enough for a rule, need or standard
forms.example: You must satisfy all the entry requirements before you can apply.

syn.note: Very close and easy: 'meet the requirements'.
Formal: 'fulfil the conditions'. American spelling: fulfill.
To be the same as or equal to what is needed.

ant.note: Here: to not reach the standard that is needed.

forms.definition: good enough for a purpose but not excellent
forms.example: Her exam results were satisfactory, but she wants to do better.
forms.note: On school reports, 'satisfactory' often means 'only just good enough'.

syn.note: Very close: good enough to accept.
Very close, a little more formal.
Informal and very common.
Easy everyday word: 'The room is fine.'
Informal: quite good; a bit more positive than satisfactory.

ant.note: Not good enough.
Too bad to be accepted.
Easy word: of low quality.

forms.definition: pleased because you have got what you wanted
forms.example: I'm satisfied with my new phone.
forms.note: Belongs to satisfaction = the good feeling, not 'good enough'.

forms.definition: giving you a pleasant feeling
forms.example: Finishing a hard puzzle is very satisfying.
forms.note: Belongs to satisfaction = the good feeling, not 'good enough'.

forms.definition: in a way that is good enough
forms.example: The problem with the water pipe was fixed satisfactorily.

syn.note: Very close, a little more formal.
In a way that is good enough to accept.
Easy word, but more positive: well means good, not just good enough.

ant.note: In a way that is not good enough.
Easy word: in a poor way.

context.text: The teacher said Bekzod's homework was satisfactory but not excellent. He hopes to satisfy the entry requirements for the university next year.

reviewer_note: Kept to the 'good enough / meet a standard' meaning: satisfy = meet requirements, satisfaction only in formal 'to someone's satisfaction'. Satisfied/satisfying are other_meaning (the good feeling).

corpus_definition: to collect money over time to buy something
particle_note: Not separated before 'for': 'save up for a car'. You can add an amount: 'save up 500 dollars for a car' or 'save up for + noun'. Also 'save up to buy something'.

relations.note: Very close and easy: 'save for a holiday'. 'Up' adds the idea of doing it over a long time.
To keep some money to use later: 'put aside some money each month'.
British, a little old-fashioned: to keep money for later.
To keep money or time for one special purpose.
To use money to buy things.
To use money badly, on things you don't need.

context.text: Jasur is saving up for a new laptop. He saved up for six months and finally bought it in Tashkent.

reviewer_note: Phrasal verb; no forms. Related noun 'savings' is not shown because phrasal maps have no forms.

corpus_definition: A tool with sharp teeth used for cutting wood or metal.

forms.definition: a tool with a metal blade with sharp teeth for cutting wood
forms.example: My uncle bought a new saw to cut wood for the winter.
forms.note: Don't confuse with saw, the past tense of see. They are different words.

syn.note: Another tool for cutting wood, but you swing it and hit. American spelling: ax.
The flat, sharp metal part of a tool or knife.
A kind of saw with a thin blade for cutting metal.

forms.definition: to cut wood or metal by moving a toothed tool back and forth
forms.example: He sawed the long board into three pieces.
forms.note: Forms: saw, sawed, sawn (or sawed).

syn.note: Easy, general word: to divide with something sharp.
To cut with strong hits, usually with an axe or knife.

forms.note: No common adjective in this family. Sawn is the past participle of the verb (sawn wood).
No adverb in this family.

context.text: Grandfather took his old saw from the shed. He sawed the dry branches into small pieces for the fire.

reviewer_note: Homonym trap: saw = past tense of see is a different word, noted on the noun. Compounds (sawdust, sawmill, chainsaw) left out.

corpus_definition: a permanent mark left on skin after a wound heals

forms.definition: a mark that stays on your skin after a cut or burn gets better
forms.example: He has a small scar on his chin from a fall when he was a child.
forms.note: Can also be used for feelings: 'The war left deep scars.'

syn.note: Easy, general word for a spot or line on a surface.
A wound is the fresh injury; it may later leave this mark.
A fresh opening in the skin, before it heals.

forms.definition: to leave a lasting mark on someone's skin
forms.example: The burn scarred her hand.
forms.note: Forms: scar, scarred, scarring (double r).

syn.note: Easy word: to leave a spot or line on something.
Stronger: to spoil how someone looks.

forms.definition: having marks on the skin from old injuries
forms.example: The old soldier's arms were scarred from the war.

syn.note: Having marks or spots on it.

ant.note: With no marks on it.

forms.note: No adverb in this family.

context.text: Timur fell off his bike and cut his knee. The cut healed, but it scarred his skin, and he still has a small scar there.

reviewer_note: Spelling trap: scarred / scarring double the r. Scary and scare are not family (different word).

corpus_definition: to throw or spread things in many different directions

forms.definition: a small number of things spread over an area
forms.example: There was a scattering of clouds in the evening sky.
forms.note: Usually 'a scattering of + plural noun'.

syn.note: Very close: a small amount spread here and there.

forms.definition: a small number of things spread around in different places
forms.example: A scatter of small houses lay along the river.
forms.note: Less common than scattering.

syn.note: A small amount spread here and there.

forms.definition: to throw or drop things so they spread over a wide area
forms.example: She scattered seeds across the garden.
forms.note: Also used without an object: 'The birds scattered when the dog ran in.'

syn.note: Easy word: to put things over a large area.
To scatter small pieces or drops, like salt or water.
Informal: to throw things carelessly in all directions.
Formal: to go or send in different directions.

ant.note: To bring things together into one place.
To bring things together.

forms.definition: spread over a wide area, not close together
forms.example: There were scattered toys all over the floor.
forms.note: Weather: 'scattered showers' means rain in a few places.

syn.note: Easy phrase: not close together.
Here and there over an area: 'dotted around the city'.

ant.note: All together in one place.

forms.note: No common adverb in this family.

context.text: The strong wind scattered the leaves across the yard. By morning there were scattered leaves everywhere, and only a scattering of them stayed on the trees.

reviewer_note: Scatterbrain is a compound and is left out.

corpus_definition: To rub your skin with your nails to stop an itch.

forms.definition: the act of rubbing your skin with your nails when it itches
forms.example: The dog sat down and had a good scratch behind its ear.
forms.note: Usually 'have a scratch' or 'give something a scratch'.

syn.note: Moving your hand on something; not always with nails.

forms.definition: a thin cut or mark on skin or on a surface
forms.example: There is a scratch on my new car door.
forms.note: Belongs to scratch = make a mark or small cut, not rubbing an itch.

forms.definition: to rub your skin with your nails because it itches
forms.example: Try not to scratch your mosquito bites.
forms.note: Also: scratch your head (to show you are thinking or confused).

syn.note: To move your hand or something on a surface; you can rub without nails.
American informal 'itch' can mean scratch, but usually itch is the feeling, not the action.

forms.definition: rough and making your skin feel itchy
forms.example: This wool jumper feels scratchy on my neck.

syn.note: Making you want to rub your skin.
Easy word: not smooth.

ant.note: Easy word: smooth and pleasant to touch.
With no rough parts.

forms.note: No adverb in this family.

context.text: My new sweater is so scratchy that I keep scratching my arms. After a good scratch, I took it off and put on a cotton shirt.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: the example 'The cat will scratch you' uses the 'cut with claws' meaning, not rubbing an itch; map follows the definition. Scratch card is a compound and is left out.

corpus_definition: A metal piece that you twist to join things together.

forms.definition: a thin pointed piece of metal that you turn to hold things together
forms.example: One screw is loose, so the shelf is falling down.

syn.note: A nail is hit with a hammer; this one is turned.
A bolt is thicker, has no point and is used with a nut.

forms.definition: to fix something in place by turning a metal pin
forms.example: He screwed the mirror to the bathroom wall.
forms.note: Also: screw on a lid (to close it by turning). Screw is also a rude slang verb; avoid it in that use.

syn.note: To join or close something firmly.
Easy word: to attach something firmly in place.
To join one thing to another.

ant.note: To take something out or off by turning it.

forms.note: No adjective in this meaning.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: Aziz needed four screws to put up the new shelf. He screwed it to the wall and placed his books on it.

reviewer_note: Screwdriver is a compound and is left out. Adjective 'screwed' (in trouble) is vulgar slang and not shown.

corpus_definition: The state of being safe from harm or danger.

forms.definition: the state of being safe and protected from danger
forms.example: The airport has strict security checks for all passengers.

syn.note: Easy and close: being safe from harm.
Being kept safe by someone or something.
Action to protect against an attack. American spelling: defense.

ant.note: Not feeling safe or sure of yourself.
The chance of being hurt or harmed.

forms.definition: to make something safe or firmly closed
forms.example: Please secure your bags before the bus leaves.

syn.note: To keep someone or something safe.
To close or fix something firmly.
Easy word: to close with a key.

forms.definition: safe and protected, so nothing bad can happen
forms.example: Keep your passport in a secure place.

syn.note: Easy and very close.
Kept safe from harm.

ant.note: Not safe or not protected.
Easy word: dangerous.
Easy to hurt or attack.

forms.definition: in a way that is safe or firmly fixed
forms.example: Make sure the door is securely locked.

syn.note: Easy word: without danger.
Tightly, so it doesn't move.

ant.note: Not tightly fixed.

context.text: Security is very important at Tashkent airport. Passengers must keep their bags secure, and staff make sure every door is securely closed.

reviewer_note: Security comes from secure; secure is both verb and adjective here. Insecure/insecurity are in ant lists. Security guard is a compound and is left out.

corpus_definition: One of two periods in a school year.

forms.definition: one of the two parts that a school or university year is divided into
forms.example: The first semester at our university ends in December.
forms.note: Common in American English and in Uzbek universities.

syn.note: Very close; common in British English. A school year may have two or three terms.
One of three parts of a school year, mostly in American English.
A period of study or a school year in some countries.

forms.note: No verb in this family.
No common adjective in this family.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: At my university in Samarkand, the spring semester starts in February. Exams take place at the end of each semester.

reviewer_note: Only one form exists; semestral is too rare for learners.
